title: Erdős #105 OQ-01: The n−4 Obstacle Question (Monotonicity Reduction)
description: Open question from Erdős #105: does the Erdős–Purdy rich-line property survive n−4 obstacles, one fewer than Xichuan's disproved n−3 case? This entry does NOT resolve it. It supplies the axiom-free structural reduction — the rich-unblocked property is antitone in the number of obstacles — that locates the question exactly: a YES pins the threshold f(n)=n−4, a NO would strengthen Xichuan's disproof. Fully verified, 0 axioms, 0 sorries.

overview.historicalContext: Erdős Problem #105 (Erdős–Purdy, 1995) asks whether n non-collinear points A in the plane, together with n−3 obstacle points B, always admit a 'rich' line — a line through ≥ 2 points of A — that avoids every obstacle. Hickerson showed the analogous n−2 statement fails; Beck and Szemerédi–Trotter (1983) showed that with only cn obstacles a rich unblocked line always exists. Xichuan (2024) disproved the n−3 conjecture with three explicit counterexamples, earning the $50 prize. This leaves a sharp frontier: the threshold function f(n) — the largest obstacle count that can always be avoided — satisfies cn ≤ f(n) ≤ n−4. OQ-01 asks whether the property holds at exactly n−4 obstacles, one fewer than the disproved case.
overview.problemStatement: Open Question 1 of Erdős #105: for all n ≥ 5, do n non-collinear points A with n−4 disjoint obstacles B always admit a line through ≥ 2 points of A avoiding all of B? Equivalently, is f(n) = n−4 (its maximum possible value given Xichuan's disproof)?
overview.text: Structural reduction for the open n−4 obstacle question of Erdős #105.
overview.proofStrategy: The question is OPEN; this file does not answer it. Instead it isolates the one structural fact that makes the question precise: obstacle-count monotonicity. The predicate RichAvoids n m (every disjoint obstacle set of size exactly m can be avoided by a rich line) is antitone in m. The single step RichAvoids n (m+1) → RichAvoids n m is proved by a padding argument: given an m-obstacle instance, place one extra obstacle in the infinite plane outside A ∪ B, solve the harder (m+1)-obstacle instance, and observe that the rich line returned avoids the original smaller obstacle set. Iterating via Nat.le_induction gives full antitonicity. The consequences place OQ-01 exactly: a positive answer forces survival at every obstacle count up to n−4 (pinning f(n)=n−4 against Xichuan's n−3 failure), while a negative answer would manufacture a fresh n−3 counterexample, strictly strengthening Xichuan's disproof.
keyInsights: More obstacles is strictly harder: surviving m+1 obstacles implies surviving m, because an avoided line for the padded set is a fortiori an avoided line for any subset.
The only non-formal ingredient is that the plane ℝ² is infinite — a finite configuration always leaves room for one more obstacle (exists_point_not_mem).
OQ-01 sits exactly one obstacle below Xichuan's disproof boundary: monotonicity shows a YES pins f(n)=n−4 and a NO strengthens the disproof, so the n−4 question is genuinely the sharp frontier.
The reduction is fully verified (0 axioms, only propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound) and self-contained, importing only Mathlib; it does not inherit the parent file's two axioms.

conclusion.summary: This entry establishes the axiom-free monotonicity reduction for the open n−4 obstacle question of Erdős #105. With 8 verified theorems, 0 axioms, and 0 sorries, it pins the open question precisely against Xichuan's n−3 disproof without resolving it.
conclusion.implications: Obstacle-count monotonicity squeezes OQ-01 to a single value: given Xichuan's f(n) ≤ n−4 and the Beck–Szemerédi–Trotter lower bound f(n) ≥ cn, a positive answer to OQ-01 is equivalent to f(n) = n−4 exactly, and a negative answer would be a strictly stronger disproof than Xichuan's. The reduction also clarifies why the n−4 case — not n−5 or lower — is the meaningful frontier.
openQuestions: Does the rich-line property actually hold with n−4 obstacles (is f(n) = n−4)?
If not, what is the exact threshold f(n) below n−4?
Can Xichuan's three n−3 counterexamples be adapted to produce an n−4 counterexample?
